title: Protecting Stored Records Can Make a Local Quantum Gate Arbitrarily Expensive
content: Local fields alone can implement a product of single-qubit phase rotations. I show that keeping old records readable in a quantum memory can make a prescribed local gate arbitrarily expensive to implement, even when the same bit can be encoded at fixed cost. In a five-qubit memory, two such products write the same bit, which a single parity measurement reads without error. One keeps every record fixed at an additional action of π/2. For the other, the exact minimum is (π/2)(2 − √(1 − η²))/η over all one- and two-qubit drives with unrestricted local diagonal fields. The tolerance 0 < η ≤ √3/4 bounds each record’s trace distance from its initial state at all times. The action diverges as 1/η, reaching fifty times the fixed-record encoder’s action at η = 0.02. In the nine-qubit Shor code the same formula holds for 0 < η ≤ 1/4 with the logical qubit free to rotate within its syndrome sector, provided the wrong-syndrome probability never exceeds η². In a seven-qubit relaxation model the prescribed gate needs at least 6.7 μs and the records allow about 2.0 μs. The alternative finishes in 0.86 μs. The choice of gate can decide whether the bit arrives in time.
